project_name: BioValue AI demo: fictional softwood kraft lignin stream
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The lignin is currently fired as internal fuel, so selling it would compete with its existing use as a substitute for purchased fuel.
The stream leaves as wet cake and no lignin dryer is available; buyers requiring dry powder would need to provide drying.
Fractionation and chemical modification equipment are not available at the mill.
Moisture is uncertain, affecting dry tonnage and the amount of material that must be shipped.
Missing molecular-weight, phenolic-hydroxyl, and sodium data limit assessment against buyer or pathway specifications.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional demo data; all figures are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from a real mill, and should not support real-world decisions.
The validation checks passed for dry-matter balance, composition total, and documentation of missing figures; no inconsistencies were reported.
The lignin-content method is stated for illustration only, and the record flags it as unclear.
Moisture is flagged as uncertain; the record recommends measuring it over time.
The record provides assumed operating ranges, which are not measured variability.
agent.summary: The fictional record reports 40000.0 t/yr wet lignin at a moisture fraction of 0.35000000000000003, yielding 26000.0 t/yr dry mass. The record is internally consistent under the reported validation checks, but the missing properties, uncertain moisture, and illustrative-only measurements prevent confident commercial qualification.

lignin_pct.method: Acid-insoluble (Klason) plus acid-soluble lignin, as % of dry matter (method stated for illustration)

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

checks.detail: recorded dry matter 26,000 t/yr; wet quantity x (1 - moisture) = 26,000 t/yr
lignin + ash + carbohydrates = 96.5% of dry matter
3 missing figure(s), each with a data-gap entry

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins for adhesives used in plywood and other wood-based panels; the reviewed literature describes activation or depolymerization before use.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is reported for veneer plywood, with a manufacturer stating that its product meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers are plywood and other wood-panel adhesive producers or users, including veneer-plywood manufacturers.

competing_materials.statement: The direct incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resin.

qualification_requirements.statement: The reviewed process calls for activation or depolymerization of kraft lignin before PF-resin use.

A manufacturer reports that its LPF resin meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood; a laboratory study reports that a resin with lignin making up half of its phenolic component met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in that study.

limitations: The reported phenol-replacement levels summarize published studies and are not results from one commercial plant (EV-PF-01).
The industrial-performance and cost claims from UPM are vendor claims, with no test report cited; the cited lignin is not characterized as kraft lignin in that document (EV-PF-02).
The lab study used poplar plywood samples; its paper names the Chinese standard inconsistently (EV-PF-04).
The IEA-cited TRL 8 refers to biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically to kraft-lignin resin (EV-PF-01).
missing_information: The evidence does not establish current lignin-resin prices, market volumes for lignin-based resin, named buyers, purchase contracts, or regional demand.
The evidence does not establish whether this fictional mill's lignin meets buyer specifications or whether its required activation or depolymerization would be economical.

market_evidence.rationale: The library contains substantial research and a vendor statement that LPF resin is industrially proven, but it does not document lignin-resin sales by a producer or named buyers. Under the rubric, documented interest and claims without documented sales support a score below the commercial-sales levels.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Lignin has been tested as a partial polyol replacement in rigid polyurethane/polyisocyanurate foams; one study found that some lignin-containing formulations passed measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications, while two of three failing foams were made with kraft lignin.

Unmodified kraft lignins have also been tested in flexible polyurethane foam; the study suggests kraft-lignin foams may suit heavy-duty uses, while organosolv lignins were judged most suitable for automotive flexible foam.
Reviews describe lignin use in polyurethane foams, panels, coatings, and rubber replacement, and report modified-kraft-lignin routes for polyol replacement.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include rigid-foam producers and flexible-foam producers, including producers of heavy-duty foams; the reviewed flexible-foam study also evaluates automotive foam applications.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material identified for polyol replacement is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: The rigid-foam study assessed formulations against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
The cited acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production is total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH); this is total OH, not phenolic OH.
The review says kraft lignin needs significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: The rigid-foam evidence comes from laboratory cup tests covering several lignin types, and the study does not give a kraft-only pass rate (EV-PU-01).
The cited rigid-foam study found lower compressive strength with lignin in general, and two of three failing foams used kraft lignin (EV-PU-01).
The flexible-foam study used laboratory one-pot foams; it did not measure the sulfur odor it identifies as a possible drawback of some softwood kraft lignins (EV-PU-03).

The TRL rating applies to a broad category of polyurethane uses, not specifically to kraft-lignin foam, and the replacement levels summarized in the review each come from a single cited study (EV-PU-04).
A 2025 review abstract reports commercialization challenges but the full text was unavailable (EV-PU-05).
missing_information: The evidence does not provide current lignin-polyol prices, market volumes for lignin-based polyurethane, named buyers, purchase contracts, or regional demand.
The evidence does not establish whether this fictional mill's lignin meets polyurethane formulation requirements; its total hydroxyl value is not supplied in the feedstock profile.
The evidence does not quantify the cost or mill-scale performance of the required lignin treatments for this feedstock.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence consists mainly of laboratory studies and reviews, with a broad TRL assessment, but it does not document a lignin-polyurethane pilot, commercial sales, or named buyers. That supports research-stage interest rather than the rubric's pilot or commercial-sales levels.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

applications.statement: Lignin is studied as a carbon-fiber precursor, but softwood lignin is reported not to be readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent, and lignin-based fiber properties in one project were about half of its target.

Kraft lignin has been studied as a precursor for hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes; a review reports higher initial coulombic efficiency for hard carbon made from kraft lignin than for hard carbon from sulfonated lignin in the cited comparison.
Lignin can also be converted into activated carbon, including lignin that is too impure for other uses; higher ash was associated with lower activated-carbon yield and carbon conversion.
A company announced a pilot production line for lignin-based anode material for lithium-ion batteries, with production planned in standardized manufacturing units.

target_customers.statement: Potential carbon-fiber customers include automotive lightweighting applications, which the cited DOE project identifies as a target for carbon-fiber mechanical properties.
Potential hard-carbon anode customers include battery manufacturers and carmakers; the company source discusses their qualification of lignin-based anode material for lithium-ion batteries.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based fiber is identified as a competing carbon-fiber material.
For hard carbon, the cited feedstock comparison includes anthracite as a competing fossil precursor.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, removal of particulates larger than 1 µm, and residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm.
The DOE project states that kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber needed purification, and that a plasticizing or alloying agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
A company source says qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years; the library provides no specific battery-anode material test standard or quality specification.

limitations: The stringent ORNL precursor specifications apply to carbon fiber, not hard carbon or activated carbon, and are cited secondhand; the carbon-fiber study used lignin from a near-neutral hemicellulose extraction process rather than standard kraft pulping (EV-CM-01).
The DOE report findings are from 2009; its mechanical targets are carbon-fiber product targets, not precursor specifications (EV-CM-02).
The GreenLight project reports its own results; its TRL 5 applies to precursor-fiber production, not the full lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain, and costs are modelled rather than measured (EV-CM-03).
The hard-carbon comparison is a review of other studies, covers sodium-ion batteries, and does not specify the currency or basis beyond '$/t' for its feedstock cost column (EV-CM-04).
The activated-carbon evidence is a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation (EV-CM-05).
The battery pilot and qualification information comes from company investor material with forward-looking statements, and the later status of its 2021 plans was not verified (EV-CM-06).
missing_information: The evidence does not establish current prices, volumes, named buyers, contracts, or regional demand for carbon products made from lignin.

The evidence does not establish whether this fictional lignin meets carbon-fiber precursor specifications; ash, volatiles, particulates, residual carbohydrate, and lignin content against the cited specifications are not established by the market evidence.

For battery hard carbon and activated carbon, the evidence does not supply buyer qualification specifications, sales or contract evidence, or a comparison of this mill's lignin with buyer requirements.
The evidence does not document commercial sales of lignin-derived carbon products by a producer.

market_evidence.rationale: The library documents a lignin-carbon-fiber development project reaching TRL 5 for precursor-fiber production and a company-announced pilot line for lignin-based battery anode material. These support the rubric's pilot or development stage, but the evidence does not document commercial sales.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before PF-resin use; the reviewed process uses a two-step route with depolymerized lignin, and the reported molecular-weight range describes the treated material, not the incoming mill stream.
The mill has no chemical-modification equipment, and the stream leaves as wet cake; drying would need to be arranged by the buyer or a new facility if dry powder is required.

The feedstock compatibility tool returned no score because the evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway; the feedstock's molecular weight, phenolic-OH, and sodium properties are also missing.

technical_maturity.statement: The evidence reports TRL 8 for biobased phenolic-resin production generally, but that rating is not specific to kraft-lignin resin.

adoption_barriers.statement: Commercial use requires treated lignin and resin qualification with adhesive producers or panel makers; the mill has no modification equipment and the evidence does not establish that this feedstock meets a buyer's requirements.
The market evidence reports a manufacturer claim for lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin but does not establish a buyer, contract, or current price for this mill's material.
Selling the lignin would displace its current internal-fuel use, and moisture uncertainty and wet-cake handling could affect usable dry supply and logistics.

drying and treatment costs for this feedstock
assumptions: Economics uses fictional scenario assumptions: wet feedstock mass of 36,000/40,000/43,000 t/yr, moisture of 40/35/30% of wet mass, and availability fraction of 40/50/60% for conservative/base/optimistic cases, respectively.

The economics tool calculated dry mass of 21,600/26,000/30,100 t/yr and usable dry feedstock of 8,640/13,000/18,060 t/yr across conservative/base/optimistic cases; product output, revenue, variable cost, and gross contribution were not calculated.
The economic scenarios are illustrative, not measured operating ranges; gross contribution would exclude capital costs, fixed costs, and the opportunity value of lignin in its current use.
No additional processing yield, price, cost, or buyer qualification outcome is assumed.
uncertainties: No TRL specific to kraft-lignin PF resin is established; the reported TRL describes biobased phenolic resins generally.
No numeric feedstock-compatibility score can be calculated from the available pathway requirements.
Product output and contribution cannot be assessed until product yield, price, and variable costs are supplied.
Moisture, feedstock characterization, treatment performance, and the value of displaced fuel use could materially change feasibility.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: The route is identifiable, but commercialization requires new activation or depolymerization capability or an as-yet-unidentified processing partner, along with buyer qualification; the mill does not have chemical-modification equipment.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 8 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-01#3.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

processing_requirements.statement: For carbon fiber, the cited precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, removal of particulates larger than 1 µm, and residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm; the compatibility tool scored this pathway 1 based on the two checked properties, lignin content and ash, with the largest relative gap reported as 900%.

The cited kraft-lignin carbon-fiber route requires purification, and softwood lignin needs a plasticizing or alloying agent to be melt-spun; the mill has no fractionation or chemical-modification equipment.

The carbon-fiber compatibility score applies only to that precursor route; the available requirements do not establish numerical compatibility for hard carbon or activated carbon, and lower ash is reported to improve activated-carbon yield.

The pathway spans distinct products and processes, including carbon fiber, battery anode material, and activated carbon; the activated-carbon study used zinc chloride activation, and buyer-specific specifications for battery hard carbon or activated carbon are not established in the supplied findings.

technical_maturity.statement: A development project reports TRL 5 for production of lignin precursor fiber, not for the full lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain or the other carbon-material routes.

adoption_barriers.statement: Carbon-fiber use faces demanding precursor specifications and purification and spinning needs; the fictional feedstock profile reports lignin content of 94% and ash of 1%, outside the checked cited limits, while several other required properties are unavailable.
The mill has no purification or chemical-modification equipment, and a carbon-fiber route would also need plasticizing/alloying and downstream processing capability or a partner.

Battery-anode qualification can be lengthy and requires customer engagement; the evidence describes a company-announced pilot but does not verify its later status or establish a specification for this feedstock.
The mill's current internal-fuel use creates an opportunity cost, while wet-cake delivery, no mill dryer, and uncertain moisture affect logistics and supply estimates.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
